Action Plan:
1. Arrange same-day face-to-face GP appointment for physical abdominal and pelvic examination, urine dipstick, and point-of-care urine pregnancy test to rule out pregnancy and other causes of lower abdominal pain.
2. If pain intensifies, new vomiting, light-headedness, fainting, heavy vaginal bleeding, or other concerning symptoms occur before the appointment, patient to seek urgent medical attention (ED/urgent care).
3. Continue adequate oral hydration; maintain usual high-fibre diet while awaiting review.
4. Record amoxicillin allergy prominently in chart; avoid prescribing penicillins.
5. Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
• 23-year-old female presents with 2–3 day history of constant dull ache below umbilicus associated with nausea and feeling hot/sweaty.  
• No vomiting, no diarrhea.  
• Bowel: constipation one week ago, now passing stools normally (last BM yesterday).  
• Urinary: drinking large volumes of water; reports increased frequency but no dysuria, urgency, malodour, or visible haematuria.  
• Gynaecology: LMP ~3 weeks ago; expects period soon; mild pink tinge noticed in urine/possible spotting over last few days; sexually active with one regular partner; uses etonogestrel implant (Implanon); pregnancy considered unlikely but not excluded. No abnormal vaginal discharge.  
• Past medical history: none reported.  
• Allergies: amoxicillin (reaction details not stated).  
• Medications: contraceptive implant (dose/route/frequency not documented).  
• Family history: brother with type 1 diabetes.  
• Social: non-smoker; lives with boyfriend.

Objective:
• Telehealth consultation; no physical examination performed.  
• Patient reports feeling febrile/hot and sweaty; denies light-headedness.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Lower abdominal pain with nausea  
   - Assessment: Undifferentiated lower abdominal pain; possible early pregnancy vs gastrointestinal (e.g., resolving constipation) vs urinary cause.  
   - Investigations planned: Same-day abdominal and pelvic examination; urine pregnancy test; further tests per in-person GP assessment (e.g., urine dip, labs, imaging if indicated).  
   - Treatment planned: Symptomatic care pending assessment; safety-net advice provided.  
   - Relevant referrals: Urgent face-to-face GP review today.

2. Increased urinary frequency  
   - Assessment: Polyuria/urinary frequency of unclear etiology (hydration vs early UTI vs hormonal).  
   - Investigations planned: Urine dipstick and culture as part of same-day review.  
   - Treatment planned: Dependent on investigation results.

3. Amoxicillin allergy  
   - Assessment: Confirmed drug allergy.  
   - Treatment planned: Avoid amoxicillin and related penicillins; document clearly in medical record.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements: No vital signs, physical examination, or detailed allergy reaction documented.  
● Internal conflicts: None noted.  
● Transcript quality: Clear; minimal background noise; no inaudible sections.
